messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Carlos

Carlos was twenty-one when his three-year-old daughter, Lucía, stopped breathing in the middle of the night. She had been feverish for two days—nothing alarming, he thought, just one of those childhood colds that passed through daycare. But at 2 a.m., his ex-partner's frantic call pulled him from sleep: Lucía was unresponsive, her lips tinged blue. The ambulance ride was a blur of sirens and his own voice breaking, begging someone—anyone—to tell him she would be okay. The hospital smelled of disinfectant and something else, something like fear itself, though he couldn't name it then. Lucía spent six days in the pediatric intensive care unit with severe pneumonia. She survived. She was discharged healthy. But Carlos did not return to the person he had been before that night.

For months afterward, he tried to move forward as though nothing fundamental had shifted. He returned to his job as a data scientist at a tech firm, where he could lose himself in code and algorithms, in problems with clean solutions. But the world had become a minefield of reminders. When an ambulance siren wailed past his apartment, Carlos's entire body seized—his heart would slam against his ribs, and within seconds his mind would fracture into that hospital night, the smell of sweat on his own skin mixing with the antiseptic reek of the ICU. The siren didn't just startle him; it pulled him back into pure terror, the same helpless dread he'd felt watching his daughter's chest barely rise and fall. Each time, the memory felt impossibly vivid and impossibly unreal at once—he could see the monitors, hear the beeping, feel the vinyl chair beneath him, yet some part of him couldn't reconcile that this had actually happened, that his daughter had actually come so close to dying.

To manage the intrusions, Carlos developed a rigid internal discipline. He would not think about that night—he simply wouldn't allow his mind to go there. When a memory began to surface, he would shut it down through sheer force of will, redirecting his attention to work, to spreadsheets, to anything concrete. But suppressing the thought only seemed to make the memories more fragmented, the sequence of events jumbled in his mind. He couldn't piece together the timeline anymore: had the fever started on a Tuesday or Wednesday? Had he called the ambulance or had his ex-partner? The uncertainty terrified him more than the clarity would have. And when those fragmented memories did break through—triggered by a siren, or by catching the scent of his own sweat after a long day at the office—the terror that flooded back was as raw as the original event. It was the same panic, the same conviction that something catastrophic was about to happen.

He had also come to believe that anger was dangerous, that if he allowed himself to feel even ordinary frustration, it would spiral into something destructive. So he suppressed that too, pushing down irritation at colleagues, swallowing his rage at the randomness of what had happened. But this suppression only amplified his hypervigilance. Unable to process his emotions, his nervous system remained locked in high alert. He couldn't fall asleep without lying awake for hours, scanning for threats, needing to stay conscious in case something went wrong again. His body remained primed for catastrophe—jumping at the ring of a phone, at a coworker's raised voice, at the unexpected sound of someone crying in the break room. Each startle fed back into his conviction that danger was imminent, which made him grip tighter to his strategy of emotional control, which kept the memories fragmented and volatile. He began avoiding hospitals entirely, refused to go to his annual physical, and felt his chest tighten whenever he heard an ambulance in the distance.

By his twenty-fifth birthday, this vigilance had begun to erode his life in concrete ways. At work, his productivity had dropped; he found himself making careless mistakes because he couldn't concentrate, too busy monitoring his internal state and the environment around him. His colleagues had noticed his withdrawal. He hadn't been on a date in nearly four years, terrified that any intimate moment might trigger the memories, and certain that he didn't deserve happiness when his daughter had come so close to being taken from him. It was only when his supervisor gently suggested he might benefit from talking to someone that Carlos finally reached out. What frightened him most was the possibility that if he stopped trying to control his thoughts and his anger, everything would collapse—that the terror would consume him entirely, or that he would hurt someone with the rage he'd been burying. What he hoped for, though he barely dared to voice it, was to sleep through the night without his body braced for disaster, and to remember his daughter's survival without feeling like he was dying himself.
